theorems.name: Markov Property
theorems.description: Definition 1.1.1: A stochastic process (X_n) is Markov if P(X_{n+1} = j | X_0, ..., X_n) = P(X_{n+1} = j | X_n)

code.lean:
import Mathlib

open BigOperators

-- Finite-state transition kernel with stochastic rows.
structure FiniteMarkovKernel (ι : Type*) [Fintype ι] where
  prob : ι → ι → ℝ
  nonnegative : ∀ i j, 0 ≤ prob i j
  row_sum : ∀ i, ∑ j, prob i j = 1

-- The conditional law of the next state for a chain generated by P depends only
-- on the last observed state in the history.
def ConditionalNextLaw {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    (P : FiniteMarkovKernel ι) (history : List ι) (next : ι) : ℝ :=
  match history.getLast? with
  | some current => P.prob current next
  | none => 0

-- Formal finite-state Markov property: adding older past before the current state
-- does not change the conditional law of the next state.
def DiscreteTimeMarkovProperty {ι : Type*}
    (condNext : List ι → ι → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (past : List ι) (current next : ι),
    condNext (past ++ [current]) next = condNext [current] next

example {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] (P : FiniteMarkovKernel ι) :
    DiscreteTimeMarkovProperty (ConditionalNextLaw P) := by
  intro past current next
  simp [DiscreteTimeMarkovProperty, ConditionalNextLaw]

example {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] (P : FiniteMarkovKernel ι) (i : ι) :
    ∑ j, P.prob i j = 1 :=
  P.row_sum i

metadata.formalization_scope: Faithful finite-state Lean encoding of the Markov-property definition: the next-state conditional law depends only on the current state, with stochastic transition rows.

theorems.name: Chapman-Kolmogorov Equation
theorems.description: Proposition 1.2.3: P^{m+n}(i,j) = sum_k P^m(i,k) P^n(k,j) — transition matrices compose by multiplication

code.lean:
import Mathlib

open Matrix BigOperators

-- Chapman-Kolmogorov for a finite-state transition matrix: the (i,j) entry of
-- P^(m+n) is the sum over intermediate states k of P^m(i,k) P^n(k,j).
example {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (P : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (m n : ℕ) (i j : ι) :
    (P ^ (m + n)) i j = ∑ k, (P ^ m) i k * (P ^ n) k j := by
  rw [pow_add]
  rw [Matrix.mul_apply]

metadata.formalization_scope: Faithful finite-state formal statement/proof of Chapman-Kolmogorov as matrix-power composition.

theorems.name: Strong Markov Property
theorems.description: Theorem 1.2.11 (strong Markov property) on trajectory space for a countable-state chain with any initial law and one-step laws P: for every stopping time τ of the natural filtration, every event C of the stopped σ-algebra 𝓕_τ and every measurable set A of trajectories, ℙ(C ∩ {τ<∞, X_τ=j, (X_{τ+m})ₘ ∈ A}) = ℙ(C ∩ {τ<∞, X_τ=j}) · ℙ_j(A), where ℙ_j is the law of the chain started at j: conditionally on {τ<∞, X_τ=j} the post-τ process is the chain started at j, independent of 𝓕_τ. Stated in this product form, with no regular conditional probability.

code.lean:
import MathFin.Probability.Discrete.MarkovPathSpace

open MathFin MeasureTheory

theorem strong_markov {ι : Type*} [MeasurableSpace ι] [MeasurableSingletonClass ι] [Countable ι]
    (init : PMF ι) (P : ι → PMF ι) {τ : (ℕ → ι) → WithTop ℕ}
    (hτ : IsStoppingTime (Filtration.piLE (X := fun _ : ℕ ↦ ι)) τ)
    {C : Set (ℕ → ι)} (hC : MeasurableSet[hτ.measurableSpace] C) (j : ι)
    {A : Set (ℕ → ι)} (hA : MeasurableSet A) :
    markovPathMeasure init P
        (C ∩ {ω | ∃ k : ℕ, τ ω = (k : WithTop ℕ) ∧ ω k = j ∧ (fun m ↦ ω (k + m)) ∈ A})
      = markovPathMeasure init P (C ∩ {ω | ∃ k : ℕ, τ ω = (k : WithTop ℕ) ∧ ω k = j})
          * markovPathMeasure (PMF.pure j) P A :=
  markovPathMeasure_strong_markov init P hτ hC j hA

Product (conditional) form; no regular conditional probability is constructed.

theorems.name: Recurrence Criterion
theorems.description: Theorem 1.3.12 (recurrence criterion), countable state space, on trajectory space: for the Ionescu–Tulcea law of the chain started at i, with one-step laws P, the chain returns to i at some positive time with probability one iff the n-step return probabilities ℙ_i(X_n = i) have infinite sum. Proved from the cylinder formula via the Markov property at the first return time and a renewal argument. The same module proves the matrix form ∑ₙ Pⁿ(i,i) = ∞ on a finite state space and the 0–1 law: ℙ_i(X_n = i infinitely often) is 1 if the sum diverges and 0 otherwise.

code.lean:
import MathFin.Probability.Discrete.MarkovPathSpace

open MathFin MeasureTheory
open scoped ENNReal

/-- Recurrence criterion on a countable state space: the chain started at `i` returns to `i` with
probability one iff `∑ₙ ℙᵢ(Xₙ = i) = ∞`. -/
theorem recurrence_criterion {ι : Type*} [MeasurableSpace ι] [MeasurableSingletonClass ι]
    [Countable ι] (P : ι → PMF ι) (i : ι) :
    markovPathMeasure (PMF.pure i) P {ω | ∃ n, 0 < n ∧ ω n = i} = 1 ↔
      ∑' n, markovPathMeasure (PMF.pure i) P {ω | ω n = i} = ∞ :=
  chainLaw_return_eq_one_iff_tsum_eq_top P i

theorems.name: Stationary Distribution Uniqueness (Finite State Space)
theorems.description: Theorem 1.4.25 for a finite state space: an irreducible row-stochastic matrix P (every state reaches every state, 0 < Pⁿ(i,j) for some n) has exactly one stationary distribution, that is one point π of the standard simplex (a probability vector) with πP = π. Uniqueness is proved by a maximum-principle argument on the positive and negative parts of the difference of two stationary vectors, existence from the convergence theorem applied to the lazy chain (I+P)/2. Positive recurrence is not a hypothesis, being automatic on a finite state space. The textbook theorem is for a countable state space; this entry proves the finite case.

code.lean:
import MathFin.Probability.Discrete.FiniteMarkovChain

open Matrix MathFin.FiniteMarkov

/-- Theorem 1.4.25 on a finite state space: an irreducible stochastic matrix has exactly one
stationary distribution. -/
theorem stationary_distribution_unique {S : Type*} [Fintype S] [DecidableEq S] [Nonempty S]
    (P : Matrix S S ℝ) (hP : P ∈ rowStochastic ℝ S) (hirr : IsIrreducible P) :
    ∃! π : Convexity.StdSimplex ℝ S, IsStationary P π :=
  existsUnique_isStationary_of_isIrreducible hP hirr

The theorem is stated for any real row-stochastic matrix; for the chain with one-step laws K : S → PMF S it applies to transitionMatrix K (MarkovPathSpace.lean), whose irreducibility is the positive-probability reachability of every state under chainLaw (isIrreducible_transitionMatrix_iff). The stationary distribution is a Convexity.StdSimplex ℝ S.

theorems.name: Ergodic Theorem for Markov Chains (finite state space, mean-square)
theorems.description: Theorem 1.4.32 (ergodic theorem), mean-square form on a finite state space: for the Markov chain with one-step laws K : S → PMF S whose real transition matrix is irreducible and aperiodic, with stationary distribution π (a point of the standard simplex), any starting state i and any f : S → ℝ, the time average (1/n) Σ_{k<n} f(X_k) converges to Σ_j π_j f(j) in L² of the path law chainLaw K i, that is E_i[((1/n) Σ_{k<n} f(X_k) − Σ_j π_j f(j))²] → 0. Proved by a variance computation from the Markov property at a fixed time and the convergence theorem Pⁿ(i,j) → π_j. The textbook's almost-sure convergence is not proved here (mean-square convergence gives convergence in probability only), aperiodicity is assumed where the textbook does not need it, and the state space is finite rather than countable with positive recurrence.

code.lean:
import MathFin.Probability.Discrete.MarkovErgodic

open MeasureTheory Filter Topology MathFin MathFin.FiniteMarkov

/-- Theorem 1.4.32 on a finite state space, in mean square: for an irreducible aperiodic chain with
stationary distribution `π`, the time averages `(1/n) ∑_{k<n} f(X_k)` converge to `∑ⱼ πⱼ f(j)` in
`L²` of the path law of the chain started at `i`. -/
theorem ergodic_theorem_mean_square {S : Type*} [Fintype S] [DecidableEq S] [MeasurableSpace S]
    [MeasurableSingletonClass S] (K : S → PMF S) (i : S)
    (hirr : IsIrreducible (transitionMatrix K)) (hap : IsAperiodic (transitionMatrix K))
    {π : Convexity.StdSimplex ℝ S} (hπ : IsStationary (transitionMatrix K) π) (f : S → ℝ) :
    Tendsto (fun n : ℕ ↦ ∫ ω, ((n : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ k ∈ Finset.range n, f (ω k)
        - ∑ j, π.weights j * f j) ^ 2 ∂chainLaw K i) atTop (𝓝 0) :=
  tendsto_integral_sq_timeAverage K i hirr hap hπ f

metadata.formalization_scope: Reduced core (special case): proved outright, in MathFin/Probability/Discrete/MarkovErgodic.lean (tendsto_integral_sq_timeAverage), for a finite state space and in mean square. The textbook theorem is almost-sure convergence of the time averages for an irreducible positive recurrent chain on a countable state space, with no aperiodicity hypothesis; here convergence is in L² (hence in probability) and the chain is aperiodic, because the proof runs through the convergence theorem Pⁿ(i,j) → π_j. The almost-sure version (by the strong Markov property and the strong law of large numbers for the i.i.d. excursions between returns, then Kac's formula for the limit) is not proved. The chain is the Ionescu–Tulcea path law chainLaw K i of one-step laws K : S → PMF S, and the matrix is transitionMatrix K.

theorems.name: Path Distribution under Markov Property
theorems.description: Theorem 1.1.2: the law of the Markov chain (init, P) assigns to every finite path the probability P(X_0=i_0,...,X_n=i_n) = init(i_0) prod_{k<n} P(i_k,i_{k+1}) — the path-distribution factorization, derived from the Ionescu-Tulcea construction.

code.lean:
import MathFin.Probability.Discrete.MarkovPathMeasure

open MeasureTheory ProbabilityTheory MathFin
open scoped ENNReal

theorem markov_path_distribution_thm {ι : Type*} [MeasurableSpace ι]
    [MeasurableSingletonClass ι] [Countable ι]
    (init : PMF ι) (P : ι → PMF ι) (path : ℕ → ι) (n : ℕ) :
    MathFin.markovPathMeasure init P (MathFin.pathCylinder path n)
      = init (path 0) * ∏ k ∈ Finset.range n, P (path k) (path (k + 1)) :=
  MathFin.markovPathMeasure_cylinder init P path n

theorems.name: Detailed Balance Implies Stationarity
theorems.description: Proposition 1.4.13: If pi and P are in detailed balance (pi_i p_{ij} = pi_j p_{ji}), then pi is invariant for P (pi P = pi)

code.lean:
import Mathlib

open BigOperators

-- Finite-state theorem: if a transition matrix P satisfies detailed balance with π
-- and every row of P sums to one, then π is stationary: (π P)_j = π_j.
example {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    (π : ι → ℝ) (P : ι → ι → ℝ)
    (hdb : ∀ i j, π i * P i j = π j * P j i)
    (hrow : ∀ i, ∑ j, P i j = 1) (j : ι) :
    ∑ i, π i * P i j = π j := by
  calc
    ∑ i, π i * P i j = ∑ i, π j * P j i := by
      apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
      intro i _
      exact hdb i j
    _ = π j * ∑ i, P j i := by
      rw [Finset.mul_sum]
    _ = π j := by
      rw [hrow j]
      ring

metadata.formalization_scope: Faithful finite-state formal statement/proof that detailed balance implies stationarity.

theorems.name: Convergence to the Stationary Distribution (Finite State Space)
theorems.description: Theorem 1.4.40 for a finite state space: for an irreducible aperiodic row-stochastic matrix P (aperiodic: the only common divisor of the return times of each state is 1) and a stationary distribution π, Pⁿ(i,j) → π_j for all i, j. Proved by Schur's theorem (irreducible and aperiodic give a power of P with all entries positive) and Doeblin's contraction of the column spreads. Positive recurrence is not a hypothesis (automatic when finite); no rate is stated. The textbook theorem is for a countable state space; this entry proves the finite case.

code.lean:
import MathFin.Probability.Discrete.FiniteMarkovChain

open Matrix Filter Topology MathFin.FiniteMarkov

/-- Theorem 1.4.40 on a finite state space: for an irreducible aperiodic stochastic matrix,
`Pⁿ(i,j) → π_j`. -/
theorem pow_tendsto_stationary {S : Type*} [Fintype S] [DecidableEq S]
    (P : Matrix S S ℝ) (hP : P ∈ rowStochastic ℝ S) (hirr : IsIrreducible P)
    (hap : IsAperiodic P) {π : Convexity.StdSimplex ℝ S} (hπ : IsStationary P π) (i j : S) :
    Tendsto (fun n : ℕ ↦ (P ^ n) i j) atTop (𝓝 (π.weights j)) :=
  tendsto_pow_of_isStationary hP hirr hap hπ i j
